regions.name: Montreal & South Shore
regions.note: Start where the harbor meets the inland journey. Ships here may be working the port or heading along the South Shore canal; a position report alone does not tell us which.

regions.name: Beauharnois & Lake St. Francis
regions.note: Two locks make this climb in two steps. Look for the short reach between the chambers, then remember: a nearby ship report does not tell us its place in the lock order.

regions.name: Massena · Eisenhower & Snell
regions.note: Meet the American pair: Snell and Eisenhower. Upbound ships pass Snell first, then climb again at Eisenhower. Check the official order of turn to follow a particular transit.

regions.name: Iroquois & Lake St. Lawrence
regions.note: Here the engineering is an adjustment, not a towering climb. The control lock carries ships past Iroquois Dam; the water-level difference varies. A shore view and a radio report tell different parts of the story.

regions.name: Thousand Islands & upper river
regions.note: Let your eye follow the open river toward Lake Ontario. Freighters share these waters with passenger boats and recreational craft, so take a moment to read the vessel name and report age.

locks.name: Saint-Lambert
locks.story: The first step inland starts here. Instead of asking an ocean-going ship to tackle the Lachine Rapids, the Seaway gives it a canal route around them. This lock, beside the Victoria Bridge crossing, begins the South Shore climb. Picture a room of water with doors at both ends: its water level changes while the ship stays afloat.
locks.access: A working facility. Public access has not been verified for this guide; choose a documented viewing location instead.

locks.name: Côte-Sainte-Catherine
locks.reach: Laprairie Basin to Lake St. Louis
locks.story: One rise behind us, another ahead. This second South Shore lock carries ships toward Lake St. Louis while the natural river follows its own course beside the canal. Trace the route on the map: the canal is the engineered detour that makes the inland journey possible.
locks.access: Verify public access with the local operator before visiting. A lock dot marks the facility, not a public entrance.

locks.name: Lower Beauharnois
locks.reach: Lake St. Louis to the intermediate pool
locks.story: Here is the first half of a two-step climb. Lower and Upper Beauharnois share the work of passing the change in level at the hydroelectric development. Find the short intermediate pool on the map: a ship leaves one water elevator before entering the next.
locks.access: No public entrance is established here by this guide. Use the official sources before planning a lockside stop.

locks.name: Upper Beauharnois
locks.story: Finish the second step and the landscape opens into the Beauharnois Canal and, farther along, Lake St. Francis. The two chambers divide a larger change in level into manageable lifts. Follow the water, then the ship: the vessel remains afloat throughout the climb.
locks.access: The map is an orientation guide. Verify permitted visitor areas separately from the operational lock.

locks.name: Bertrand H. Snell
locks.reach: Lake St. Francis to Wiley–Dondero Canal
locks.story: For an upbound ship, this is the first American step. Snell raises it from the Lake St. Francis side into the Wiley–Dondero Canal, with Eisenhower still ahead. Follow the route between them, but keep the timetable separate: a nearby ship is not a confirmed next arrival.
locks.access: Use the Eisenhower visitor center for the documented public lock-viewing experience. This dot is not an invitation to enter Snell's working grounds.

locks.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
locks.reach: Wiley–Dondero Canal to Lake St. Lawrence
locks.story: Pick a mark on the concrete wall and keep your eye on a railing aboard the ship. As the chamber fills or empties, the ship moves past that fixed reference. That is the trick: change the water level and the floating ship comes along. Upbound rises toward Lake St. Lawrence; downbound descends toward Snell and Montreal.
locks.access: Public observation decks at the Seaway Visitor Center, 76 Barnhart Island Road, Massena. Check the operator's current hours before driving.

locks.name: Iroquois
locks.reach: Lake St. Lawrence toward Lake Ontario
locks.story: Not every step needs to be a giant one. Iroquois is a control lock: it provides passage around the dam and adjusts between nearby water levels. Its lift varies, which is why the model uses an illustrative value. Watch for the careful passage as well as the change in height.
locks.access: South Dundas documents ship watching, green space and parking at Iroquois Point. Follow the public access signs.

viewpoints.name: Seaway Visitor Center
viewpoints.description: Give yourself a front-row seat to a floating elevator. From the public observation decks, compare the ship with a fixed point on the lock wall as its level changes. Then head inside for exhibits and a ship-handling simulator that put the river’s engineering in your hands.
viewpoints.practical: 76 Barnhart Island Road, Massena. Free admission. The operator currently lists 9 a.m.–5 p.m.; daily Memorial Day–Labor Day, Wednesday–Sunday outside peak season. Confirm current access before setting out.
viewpoints.fallback: Between ships, try a little detective work: which gate would an upbound ship enter, and where would the water need to go? The exhibits, gates and lock walls give you plenty to investigate. The center describes a typical visit as about 1½ hours.
viewpoints.access: The operator lists an accessible building and accessible restrooms. Check deck access and any temporary restrictions with the center.
viewpoints.directionsQuery: Seaway Visitor Center 76 Barnhart Island Road Massena NY

viewpoints.name: Iroquois Point
viewpoints.description: Settle into the green space beside the water and let the river set the pace. Here the story is the approach and careful passage of a large vessel through a control lock, rather than a dramatic high lift. Bring binoculars if you have them, and leave time to look.
viewpoints.practical: South Dundas identifies a parking area and open green space for ship watching at Iroquois Point. Seasonal facilities, exact access and any closures should be checked locally.
viewpoints.fallback: A quiet screen does not mean an empty river. Make this a landscape-reading stop: find the lock, follow the approaches and consider why a ship needs a way around the dam. Stay in the signed public viewing areas.
viewpoints.access: Public attraction documented by South Dundas; accessible paths, restrooms and opening hours have not been verified in this guide.

cameras.name: Alexandria Bay · River view
cameras.note: An operator-published view of the St. Lawrence River at Alexandria Bay, New York. This is an upper-river view, not a lock camera.

cameras.name: Alexandria Bay · Docks
cameras.note: The Chamber’s dock camera gives a second view of the Alexandria Bay waterfront. Docks, passing boats and the shipping channel are different things; the camera does not establish a ship’s route.

cameras.name: Brockville · City Hall south view
cameras.note: The City identifies this as the view from the back of City Hall facing the St. Lawrence River in Brockville, Ontario.

cameras.name: Brockville · Blockhouse Island west view
cameras.note: The City identifies this west-facing camera at the end of Blockhouse Island. Watch the operator’s live indicator; visibility and camera direction can change.
